papers.title: Interfacing Superconductor and Semiconductor Digital Electronics
papers.abstract: Interface circuits are the key components that enable the hybrid integration of superconductor and semiconductor digital electronics. The design requirements of superconductor-semiconductor interface circuits vary depending on the application, such as high-performance classical computing, superconducting quantum computing, and digital signal processing. In this survey, various interface circuits are categorized based on the working principle and structure. The superconducting output drivers are explored, which are capable of converting and amplifying, e.g., single flux quantum (SFQ) voltage pulses, to voltage levels that semiconductor circuits can process. Several trade-offs between circuit- and system-level design parameters are examined. Accordingly, parameters such as the data rate, output voltage, power dissipation, layout area, thermal/heat load of cryogenic cables, and bit-error rate are considered.

similar_to.title: A Review of Design Concerns in Superconducting Quantum Circuits
A Quantum Engineer's Guide to Superconducting Qubits

summary.summary: This survey reviews superconductor-semiconductor interface circuits, focusing on output drivers that convert single-flux-quantum (SFQ) pulses (1 mV, 2 ps duration) into voltage signals processable by CMOS (hundreds of mV to volts). Two main categories are identified: Josephson-junction-based drivers (latching and SQUID-based) and multi-terminal devices (cryotrons and superconductor-based transistors).
summary.motivation: Hybrid integration of superconductor and semiconductor electronics is essential for emerging applications including high-performance computing with SFQ logic operating at 57.2 GHz with 11.2 mW power, superconducting qubit control using SFQ technology for ultra-low-power readout, and direct RF signal digitization in software-defined radios.
summary.method: A taxonomy of output drivers is presented with detailed analysis of working principles: latching drivers (4JL gates, Suzuki stacks, HUFFLE), SQUID-based drivers (SQUID stacks, SFQ-to-DC converters, voltage doublers), and multi-terminal devices (nanocryotrons producing 100 mV to 8.1 V, heater-cryotrons, wire-based cryotrons). Circuit-level and system-level performance parameters including output voltage, data rate, power dissipation, layout area, and bit-error rate are compared.
summary.result: Trade-offs are identified: Suzuki stacks achieve tens to hundreds of millivolts at a few Gbps; SQUID stacks reach 20–30 Gbps with <10 mV output; SFQ-to-DC converters support up to 40–50 Gbps but produce ~1 mV; cryotrons exceed 1 V but operate below 1 GHz. State-of-the-art implementations demonstrate bit-error rates below $10^{-12}$ at 10–20 Gbps for SQUID stacks and 1–5 Gbps for Suzuki stacks.

papers.title: Coherence Limits in Interference-Based cos(2$\varphi$) Qubits
papers.abstract: We investigate the coherence properties of parity-protected $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubits based on interferences between two Josephson elements in a superconducting loop. We show that qubit implementations of a $\cos(2\varphi)$ potential using a single loop, such as those employing semiconducting junctions, rhombus circuits, flowermon and KITE structures, can be described by the same Hamiltonian as two multi-harmonic Josephson junctions in a SQUID geometry. We find that, despite the parity protection arising from the suppression of single Cooper pair tunneling, there exists a fundamental trade-off between charge and flux noise dephasing channels. Using numerical simulations, we examine how relaxation and dephasing rates depend on external flux and circuit parameters, and we identify the best compromise for maximum coherence. With currently existing circuit parameters, the qubit lifetime $T_1$ can exceed milliseconds while the dephasing time $T_\varphi$ remains limited to only a few microseconds due to either flux or charge noise. Our findings establish practical limits on the coherence of this class of qubits and raise questions about the long-term potential of this approach.

similar_to.title: The high-coherence fluxonium qubit
Millisecond coherence in a superconducting qubit

summary.summary: This paper investigates coherence properties of parity-protected $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubits based on interference between Josephson elements in a superconducting loop, showing that despite suppressing single Cooper pair tunneling for energy relaxation protection, a fundamental trade-off exists between charge and flux noise dephasing. With current circuit parameters, $T_1$ exceeds milliseconds while $T_\varphi$ remains limited to microseconds, establishing practical constraints on this qubit class.
summary.motivation: Although $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubits promise protection against energy relaxation via parity conservation, only a handful of experiments have demonstrated this protection and none have combined it with dephasing protection, motivating a comprehensive investigation of decoherence mechanisms in interference-based implementations.
summary.method: Using numerical simulations with scQubits and QuTiP, the authors analyzed a generic SQUID model with two bi-harmonic Josephson junctions across realistic material platforms (semiconductors, superconducting circuits, heterostructures), systematically exploring how relaxation and dephasing rates depend on external flux $\delta\Phi$, junction asymmetry $d$, and the ratios $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_{J\Sigma 1}$ and $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_C$.
summary.result: Optimal coherence with $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_{J\Sigma 1}\approx-0.1$ yields $T_2\sim$ few microseconds limited by charge noise at low $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_C$ and flux noise at high $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_C$; even at $E_{J\Sigma 2}/E_{J\Sigma 1}=-250$ (two orders of magnitude beyond current implementations), projections reach only $T_2\sim 20$ ms, substantially below state-of-the-art transmon coherence times.

papers.title: Hybrid superinductance with Al/InAs
papers.abstract: We report microwave spectroscopy of Josephson junctions chains made from an epitaxial Al/InAs heterostructure. The chains exhibit superinductance, with characteristic wave impedance exceeding $R_{Q} = \hbar/(2e)^{2}$. The planar nature of the junctions results in a large plasma frequency, with no measurable deviations from ideal dispersion up to $12~\mathrm{GHz}$. Internal quality factors decrease sharply with frequency, which we describe with a simple loss model. The possibility of a loss mechanism intrinsic to the superconductor-semiconductor junction is considered.

similar_to.title: Quasiparticle dynamics in epitaxial Al-InAs planar Josephson junctions
Granular aluminum: A superconducting material for high impedance quantum circuits

summary.summary: Planar Al/InAs Josephson junction chains achieve superinductance with characteristic impedance $Z = 4.7$ to $5.2~	ext{k}\ \
summary.motivation: High-impedance superconducting circuits like fluxonium require superinductors, but tunnel junctions face a conflict: small charging energy $E_C \ll E_J$ minimizes phase slips but reduces plasma frequency $\omega_p \sim \sqrt{E_C E_J}$, whereas hybrid superconductor-semiconductor junctions could potentially evade this constraint through high transparency despite $E_C > E_J$.
summary.method: Arrays of 800 planar Al/InAs junctions with lengths $l_J = 400$ or $700$ nm were fabricated on epitaxial InAs 2D electron gas (mobility $1.5 \times 10^4~\mathrm{cm}^2/\mathrm{Vs}$, density $9.76 \times 10^{11}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$), coupled capacitively to a coplanar waveguide, and characterized via microwave spectroscopy and two-tone cross-Kerr measurements at $23~\mathrm{mK}$.
summary.result: Devices with $l_J = 700$ nm exhibit $Z > R_Q$ (4.7–5.2 kΩ vs 1.03 kΩ), linear mode dispersion to $12~\mathrm{GHz}$ with junction inductance $1.8$–$2.14~\mathrm{nH}$ per unit cell, negligible shunt capacitance, but internal quality factors decay as $Q_i \propto 1/f_r$, decreasing an order of magnitude from 1–10 GHz; fitted shunt resistance $R_J \approx 10$–$11~\mathrm{k}\Omega$ (700 nm) or $3~\mathrm{k}\Omega$ (400 nm) is attributed to diffusive-junction loss.

papers.title: Experimental Realization of Rabi-Driven Reset for Fast Cooling of a High-Q Cavity
papers.abstract: High-Q bosonic memories are central to hardware-efficient quantum error correction, but their isolation makes fast, high-fidelity reset a persistent bottleneck. Existing approaches either rely on weak intermode cross-Kerr conversion or on measurement-based sequences with substantial latency. Here we demonstrate a hardware-efficient Rabi-Driven Reset (RDR) that implements continuous, measurement-free cooling of a superconducting cavity mode. A strong resonant Rabi drive on a transmon, together with sideband drives on the memory and readout modes detuned by the Rabi frequency, converts the dispersive interaction into an effective Jaynes-Cummings coupling between the qubit dressed states and each mode. This realizes a tunable dissipation channel from the memory to the cold readout bath. Crucially, the engineered coupling scales with the qubit-mode dispersive interaction and the drive amplitude, rather than with the intermode cross-Kerr, enabling fast cooling even in very weakly coupled architectures that deliberately suppress direct mode-mode coupling. We demonstrate RDR of a single photon with a decay time of $1.2 μs$, more than two orders of magnitude faster than the intrinsic lifetime. Furthermore, we reset about 30 thermal photons in about $80 μs$ to a steady-state average photon number of $\bar{n} = 0.045 \pm 0.025$.

similar_to.title: On-demand driven dissipation for cavity reset and cooling
Fast Reset and Suppressing Spontaneous Emission of a Superconducting Qubit

summary.summary: This work demonstrates Rabi-Driven Reset (RDR), a measurement-free continuous cooling protocol for a superconducting cavity mode that achieves single-photon decay in $1.2$ µs (170× faster than the intrinsic $170$ µs lifetime) and cools $\sim 30$ thermal photons to $\bar{n} = 0.045 \pm 0.025$ in $80$ µs. The method combines a strong Rabi drive on a transmon qubit with sideband drives on memory and readout modes detuned by the Rabi frequency to convert dispersive coupling into effective Jaynes–Cummings interactions, creating engineered dissipation that scales with qubit-mode coupling rather than intermode cross-Kerr.
summary.motivation: High-Q bosonic memories essential for hardware-efficient quantum error correction are isolated from the environment, creating a bottleneck for fast reset—existing methods either rely on weak cross-Kerr conversion or measurement-based sequences with substantial latency.
summary.method: A strong resonant Rabi drive ($\Omega_R / 2\pi = 9$ MHz) on a transmon qubit ($\omega_q / 2\pi = 6.33$ GHz, $E_C / 2\pi = 265$ MHz, $T_1 = 25$ µs) is applied together with sideband drives on a memory cavity ($\omega_m / 2\pi = 6.914$ GHz, $\kappa_m^{-1} = 170$ µs, $2\chi_m / 2\pi = 57$ kHz) and readout mode ($\omega_r / 2\pi = 7.7$ GHz, $\kappa_r / 2\pi = 0.382$ MHz, $2\chi_r / 2\pi = 0.635$ MHz) detuned by $\Omega_R$ to engineer dissipation without measurement.
summary.result: Maximum cooling rates of $d\bar{n}/dt = -0.73 \pm 0.08$ MHz (at $\bar{a}_m \chi_m = \kappa/2$) are achieved, limited by the readout linewidth; a single Fock state is cooled to vacuum with 93% fidelity, and the coupling rate scales with the dispersive interaction independently of intermode cross-Kerr, enabling fast cooling in weakly coupled architectures.

papers.title: Bridging Superconducting and Neutral-Atom Platforms for Efficient Fault-Tolerant Quantum Architectures
papers.abstract: The transition to the fault-tolerant era exposes the limitations of homogeneous quantum systems, where no single qubit modality simultaneously offers optimal operation speed, connectivity, and scalability. In this work, we propose a strategic approach to Heterogeneous Quantum Architectures (HQA) that synthesizes the distinct advantages of the superconducting (SC) and neutral atom (NA) platforms. We explore two architectural role assignment strategies based on hardware characteristics: (1) We offload the latency-critical Magic State Factory (MSF) to fast SC devices while performing computation on scalable NA arrays, a design we term MagicAcc, which effectively mitigates the resource-preparation bottleneck. (2) We explore a Memory-Compute Separation (MCSep) paradigm that utilizes NA arrays for high-density qLDPC memory storage and SC devices for fast surface-code processing. Our evaluation, based on a comprehensive end-to-end cost model, demonstrates that principled heterogeneity yields significant performance gains. Specifically, our designs achieve $752\times$ speedup over NA-only baselines on average and reduce the physical qubit footprint by over $10\times$ compared to SC-only systems. These results chart a clear pathway for leveraging cross-modality interconnects to optimize the space-time efficiency of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

similar_to.title: Fault-tolerant interfaces for modular quantum computing on diverse qubit platforms
Logic gates at the surface code threshold: Superconducting qubits poised for fault-tolerant quantum computing

summary.summary: This paper proposes heterogeneous quantum architectures (HQA) pairing superconducting and neutral-atom platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computing, introducing two design strategies: MagicAcc offloads magic state factories to fast SC devices ($10–100$ ns gates, 99.9% fidelity) while executing computation on scalable NA arrays ($0.1–1$ µs gates, >6000 qubits), and Memory-Compute Separation utilizes NA qLDPC memory for high-density storage while SC provides fast surface-code processing. End-to-end cost modeling demonstrates that HT-MCSep-MAcc achieves $752 ×$ speedup over NA-only baselines and reduces physical qubit footprint by $10.8 ×$ compared to SC-only systems through principled role assignment based on complementary hardware strengths.
summary.motivation: No single qubit modality simultaneously offers optimal operation speed, connectivity, and scalability for FTQC; breakthroughs in quantum interconnects make cross-platform integration viable, enabling specialization analogous to classical heterogeneous computing.
summary.method: We develop a comprehensive HQ-ISA instruction set and parameterized cost model (Sec. IV) for compute, memory, magic-state factories, and cross-modality transport, then analyze speedup via Amdahl-style formulations (Eq. 4 with drivers $S$, $r_T$, $\rho_{\mathrm{MS}}$, $P_{\mathrm{Trans}}$) and space-time trade-offs to map workload properties to optimal architectures.
summary.result: HT-MCSep-MAcc (NA qLDPC memory + NA GBC compute with SC MSF) achieves $237 ×$ speedup over homogeneous NA-MCSep and $10.8 ×$ space reduction relative to SC-only systems, with speedup saturation at $1 + \rho_{\mathrm{MS}}$ where $\rho_{\mathrm{MS}} \approx 1200$ for magic-state cultivation; transport latency up to $10^{-3}$ s remains tolerable.

papers.title: Multiple Andreev Reflection Effects in Asymmetric STM Josephson Junctions
papers.abstract: We have examined the electrical behavior of Josephson junctions formed by a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) with a Nb sample and a Nb tip, with normal-state resistances Rn varying between 1 kOhm and 10 MOhm. Current-voltage characteristics were obtained as a function of Rn by varying the distance between the tip and sample at temperatures of 50 mK and 1.5 K. Rn decreases as the tip-sample separation is reduced, and the junction evolves from a phase-diffusion regime to an underdamped small junction regime, and then to a point contact regime. The subgap structure exhibits pronounced multiple Andreev reflection (MAR) features whose amplitudes and onset energies depend sensitively on junction transparency and gap asymmetry. To interpret these spectra, we generalize the Averin-Bardas MAR theory to superconductors with unequal gap magnitudes, providing a quantitative model appropriate for asymmetric STM junctions. The resulting fits yield the superconducting gaps of the electrodes, barrier transparency, and number of conduction channels as a function of Rn. Combining this analysis with Josephson junction dynamics, we further account for the observed switching and retrapping currents and the finite resistance of the supercurrent branch. Our results demonstrate that incorporating intrinsic electrode asymmetry is essential for reliably extracting transport parameters in STM-based superconducting weak links.

similar_to.title: Electrical post-fabrication tuning of aluminum Josephson junctions at room temperature
Quasiparticle dynamics in epitaxial Al-InAs planar Josephson junctions

summary.summary: This work generalizes multiple Andreev reflection (MAR) theory to asymmetric Josephson junctions with unequal superconducting gaps, enabling quantitative interpretation of STM-based Nb–Nb junctions across three transport regimes. By measuring $I$–$V$ characteristics over normal-state resistances $R_n = 1$ kΩ to 10 MΩ at 50 mK and 1.5 K, the authors extract the tip and sample gaps ($\Delta_t \approx 0.67$ meV, $\Delta_s \approx 1.51$ meV), barrier transparency ($D$ ranging from 0.1 to 0.6), and effective channel number ($N = 2$ to 20).
summary.motivation: Josephson STM junctions commonly exhibit gap asymmetry from tip oxidation or preparation-induced variations, yet existing symmetric MAR models fail to reliably extract transport parameters; understanding asymmetric MAR is crucial for interpreting superconducting STM spectroscopy and small-junction physics in qubits.
summary.method: The authors generalized the Averin–Bardas MAR formalism to different gaps at left and right Andreev interfaces, deriving recursion relations for wavefunction amplitudes and the dc current via Eq. (8). They fit voltage- and current-biased $I(V)$ and $dI/dV$ data using a simplified model with $N$ identical channels of transparency $D$, yielding gaps and transport properties; junction dynamics were analyzed using the RCSJ model with capacitance values of order fF.
summary.result: The extracted tip gap decreased $\sim 15\%$ from $R_n = 57$ kΩ to 1 kΩ, indicating pressure or heating effects; switching current was suppressed to 1–10% of the MAR-predicted critical current $I_c$ for $10$ kΩ $< R_n < 100$ kΩ, consistent with phase diffusion; supercurrent branch resistance scaled as $R_z \propto R_n^2$ at both temperatures, agreeing with thermal Nyquist noise theory predicting $Z_1 \sim 800$–1800 Ω.

papers.title: Minimal-Energy Optimal Control of Tunable Two-Qubit Gates in Superconducting Platforms Using Continuous Dynamical Decoupling
papers.abstract: We present a unified scheme for generating high-fidelity entangling gates in superconducting platforms by continuous dynamical decoupling (CDD) combined with variational minimal-energy optimal control. During the CDD stage, we suppress residual couplings, calibration drifting, and quasistatic noise, resulting in a stable effective Hamiltonian that preserves the designed ZZ interaction intended for producing tunable couplers. In this stable $\mathrm{SU}(4)$ manifold, we calculate smooth low-energy single-quibt control functions using a variational geodesic optimization process that directly minimizes gate infidelity. We illustrate the methodology by applying it to CZ, CX, and generic engangling gates, achieving virtually unit fidelity and robustness under restricted single-qubit action, with experimentally realistic control fields. These results establish CDD-enhanced variational geometric optimal control as a practical and noise-resilient scheme for designing superconducting entangling gates.

similar_to.title: Dynamical decoupling for superconducting qubits: a performance survey
The superconducting grid-states qubit

summary.summary: This work presents a two-stage scheme combining continuous dynamical decoupling (CDD) with sub-Riemannian geodesic optimal control to generate high-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates in superconducting platforms. The CDD stage suppresses residual couplings and slow noise while preserving the designed $J_{3,3}$ ZZ coupling, followed by variational optimization using a backward-propagated adjoint equation to determine minimal-energy control fields.
summary.motivation: Superconducting two-qubit gates suffer from calibration drift, low-frequency flux noise, residual ZZ crosstalk, and leakage that resist conventional echo-based corrections and require multiple correction layers. A unified systematic control scheme that addresses these issues simultaneously while maintaining simplicity is needed.
summary.method: The approach uses CDD with modified exponential factors ($3\omega$ and $8\omega$ frequencies) to transform the native Hamiltonian into an effective stable $\mathrm{SU}(4)$ drift Hamiltonian containing only $J_{3,3}/2\pi = 82.5$ MHz ZZ interactions. Then, single-qubit control fields are optimized via three independent methods: a variational scheme based on Pontryagin's maximum principle with adjoint sensitivity analysis, a Monte Carlo costate sampling approach, and the Krotov method, all minimizing gate infidelity while constraining energy expenditure.
summary.result: CDD achieves fidelities $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{CDD}} \approx 0.99998$ at $\omega/2\pi = 20$ GHz; variational and Monte Carlo geodesic methods reach virtually unit fidelity for CZ, CX, and generic entangling gates with energetic costs $\sim 3$–$6\,\hbar^2/\tau$ depending on gate type and control restrictions, while remaining robust even when one control direction is suppressed (energetic cost increasing to $\sim 6$–$12\,\hbar^2/\tau$).

papers.title: Learning to Decode in Parallel: Self-Coordinating Neural Network for Real-Time Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract: Fast, reliable decoders are pivotal components for enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). Neural network decoders like AlphaQubit have demonstrated potential, achieving higher accuracy than traditional human-designed decoding algorithms. However, existing implementations of neural network decoders lack the parallelism required to decode the syndrome stream generated by a superconducting logical qubit in real time. Moreover, integrating AlphaQubit with sliding window-based parallel decoding schemes presents non-trivial challenges: AlphaQubit is trained solely to output a single bit corresponding to the global logical correction for an entire memory experiment, rather than local physical corrections that can be easily integrated. We address this issue by training a recurrent, transformer-based neural network specifically tailored for parallel window decoding. While it still outputs a single bit, we derive training labels from a consistent set of local corrections and train on various types of decoding windows simultaneously. This approach enables the network to self-coordinate across neighboring windows, facilitating high-accuracy parallel decoding of arbitrarily long memory experiments. As a result, we overcome the throughput bottleneck that previously precluded the use of AlphaQubit-type decoders in FTQC. Our work presents the first scalable, neural-network-based parallel decoding framework that simultaneously achieves SOTA accuracy and the stringent throughput required for real-time quantum error correction. Using an end-to-end experimental workflow, we benchmark our decoder on the Zuchongzhi 3.2 superconducting quantum processor on surface codes with distances up to 7, demonstrating its superior accuracy. Moreover, we demonstrate that, using our approach, a single TPU v6e is capable of decoding surface codes with distances up to 25 within 1us per decoding round.

similar_to.title: Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit
Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even

summary.summary: This work presents a scalable parallel neural network decoder for surface codes that achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while enabling real-time decoding throughput by training a recurrent transformer to output local logical corrections per decoding window that self-coordinate across boundaries. A single TPU v6e achieves <1 μs per syndrome round for surface codes up to distance 25, compared to AlphaQubit's ~20 μs latency, validated experimentally on the Zuchongzhi 3.2 superconducting processor achieving logical error rates of 0.0078 ± 0.0001 per round at d=7.
summary.motivation: AlphaQubit-type neural decoders exceed traditional decoders like MWPM in accuracy but incur 20–48 μs latency per syndrome round, far exceeding the ~1 μs throughput requirement for real-time fault-tolerant quantum computation on superconducting platforms. Existing parallel decoders require local physical error corrections at window seams, incompatible with AlphaQubit's global logical output.
summary.method: A recurrent transformer architecture processes syndrome windows with buffer regions (size d) and core regions (size d), trained jointly across initial, bulk, and final window types. Ground truth labels $y_i = |\mathcal{E} \cap E_i^c \cap L| \bmod 2$ are derived from consistent error sets, enabling self-coordination. Multi-layer recurrent training (Eq. 4) with truncated core sizes, DEM-based fine-tuning, and end-to-end optimization via differentiable Soft-XOR (Eq. 5) complete the framework.
summary.result: On Zuchongzhi 3.2, per-round logical error rates are 0.01451 ± 0.00004 (d=3), 0.00971 ± 0.00005 (d=5), and 0.00783 ± 0.0001 (d=7), outperforming PyMatching, Belief-Matching, and Correlated-Matching. Fault-tolerance threshold reaches 0.76% versus 0.62% for MWPM. Throughput scales to d=25 at 0.979 ± 0.021 μs per round on TPU v6e, sustaining constant latency for arbitrarily long memory experiments.

papers.title: Erasure conversion for singlet-triplet spin qubits enables high-performance shuttling-based quantum error correction
papers.abstract: Fast and high fidelity shuttling of spin qubits has been demonstrated in semiconductor quantum dot devices. Several architectures based on shuttling have been proposed; it has been suggested that singlet-triplet (dual-spin) qubits could be optimal for the highest shuttling fidelities. Here we present a fault-tolerant framework for quantum error correction based on such dual-spin qubits, establishing them as a natural realisation of erasure qubits within semiconductor architectures. We introduce a hardware-efficient leakage-detection protocol that automatically projects leaked qubits back onto the computational subspace, without the need for measurement feedback or increased classical control overheads. When combined with the XZZX surface code and leakage-aware decoding, we demonstrate a twofold increase in the error correction threshold and achieve orders-of-magnitude reductions in logical error rates. This establishes the singlet-triplet encoding as a practical route toward high-fidelity shuttling and erasure-based, fault-tolerant quantum computation in semiconductor devices.

similar_to.title: Fast, High-Fidelity Erasure Detection of Dual-Rail Qubits with Symmetrically Coupled Readout
Realizing Repeated Quantum Error Correction in a Distance-Three Surface Code

summary.summary: This paper presents a fault-tolerant quantum error correction framework based on singlet-triplet (dual-spin) qubits in semiconductor devices, establishing them as natural erasure qubits. A hardware-efficient leakage-detection protocol projects leaked qubits back to the computational subspace without measurement feedback, and when combined with the XZZX surface code achieves a twofold threshold increase and orders-of-magnitude logical error rate reductions.
summary.motivation: Singlet-triplet qubits are intrinsically protected against phase noise and support high-fidelity shuttling (demonstrated at 99.99% per increment), making them attractive for scalable shuttling-based architectures. However, their leakage out of the odd-parity computational subspace must be detected and corrected without introducing excessive overhead.
summary.method: The work designs stabilizer circuits using exchange gates (H, CZ) and driven gates (CNOT) that convert Pauli errors into detectable leakage. An erasure-detection circuit unitarily transfers state to a fresh pair and measures the old pair, automatically projecting leakage back without feedback. Two implementations are analyzed: exchange-only circuits yielding balanced $X/Z$/erasure noise, and CNOT-based circuits achieving bias-preserving $Z$-dominant noise for use with the XZZX surface code.
summary.result: Simulations show the singlet-triplet CSS encoding achieves threshold $p_c = 0.49\%$ versus $0.45\%$ for Loss-DiVincenzo qubits, while the XZZX variant reaches $p_c = 1.3\%$. At equal electron count and $p_\mathrm{sh,LD} = 0.5\%$ shuttling error (10 μm shuttling), the ST+XZZX scheme delivers orders-of-magnitude lower logical error rates when $p_\mathrm{sh,ST} \leq p_\mathrm{sh,LD}$, with effective distances benefiting from the reduced resource overhead per dual-spin qubit.

papers.title: Effects of Integrated Heatsinking on Superconductivity in Tantalum Nitride Nanowires at the 300 Millimeter Scale
papers.abstract: We report the superconducting properties of tantalum nitride (TaN) nanowires and TaN/copper (TaN/Cu) bilayer nanowires fabricated on 300 mm silicon wafers using CMOS-compatible processes. We evaluate how an integrated Cu heatsink modifies the superconducting response of TaN nanowires by improving thermal dissipation without significantly compromising key superconducting parameters. Through analysis of hysteresis in current-voltage curves, we demonstrate that Cu integration improves heat dissipation, supporting expectations of faster reset times in superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs), consistent with enhanced heat transfer away from the hot spot. Using the Skocpol-Beasley-Tinkham (SBT) hotspot model, we quantify the Cu-enabled improvement in heat transfer as an approximately 100x increase in the SBT slope parameter beta and effective interfacial heat-transfer efficiency compared to TaN nanowires. The near-unity ratio of critical to retrapping current in TaN/Cu bilayer nanowires provides another evidence of efficient heat removal enabled by the integrated Cu layer. Our results show a zero-temperature Ginzburg-Landau coherence length of 7 nm and a critical temperature of 4.1 K for 39 nm thick TaN nanowires. The nanowires show <5% variation in critical dimensions, room-temperature resistance, residual resistance ratio, critical temperature, and critical current across the 300 mm wafer for all measured linewidths, demonstrating excellent process uniformity and scalability. These results indicate the trade-offs between superconducting performance and heat-sinking efficiency in TaN/Cu bilayer nanowires. They also underscore the viability of wafer-scale fabrication for fast, large-area SNSPD arrays for applications in photonic quantum computing, cosmology, and neuromorphic computing devices.

similar_to.title: Tantalum as a base material for superconducting integrated circuits
Assessing the Sensitivity of Niobium- and Tantalum-Based Superconducting Qubits to Infrared Radiation

summary.summary: TaN and TaN/Cu bilayer nanowires were fabricated on 300 mm wafers using CMOS-compatible processes, achieving $T_c = 4.1$ K and coherence length $lap{aise 0.25em\hbox{$lap{-}$}}\xi_0 = 7$ nm for 39 nm thick TaN with <5% variation across the wafer. Cu integration provides ~100× enhancement in the SBT heat-transfer parameter $\beta$ and near-unity critical-to-retrapping current ratio, enabling faster reset times in SNSPDs while maintaining superconducting performance.
summary.motivation: Wafer-scale SNSPD arrays require fast reset times and uniform superconducting properties across large areas, motivating investigation of integrated heatsinking in TaN nanowires fabricated with scalable CMOS-compatible processes.
summary.method: TaN and TaN/Cu bilayer nanowires were patterned on 300 mm Si wafers and characterized through current-voltage hysteresis measurements and Skocpol-Beasley-Tinkham hotspot model analysis to evaluate thermal dissipation and superconducting parameters.
summary.result: Cu heatsinking improved heat transfer by ~100× (SBT $\beta$ parameter) with critical current uniformity better than 5% across the 300 mm wafer for all measured linewidths, demonstrating process viability for scalable SNSPD fabrication.
